definition: Interior-point methods (also referred to as barrier methods or IPMs) are algorithms for solving linear and non-linear convex optimization problems.
details: IPMs combine two advantages of previously-known algorithms: Theoretically, their run-time is polynomial—in contrast to the simplex method, which has exponential run-time in the worst case. Practically, they run as fast as the simplex method—in contrast to the ellipsoid method, which has polynomial run-time in theory but is very slow in practice. In contrast to active-set methods (such as the simplex method) which traverses the boundary of the feasible region, and the ellipsoid method which bounds the feasible region from outside, an IPM reaches a best solution by traversing the interior of the feasible region—hence the name.

explainer.lead: Interior-point methods are algorithms for solving linear and non-linear convex optimisation problems. They matter because they combine polynomial worst-case run-time with practical speed comparable to the simplex method.

tiers.eli5: Instead of walking around the edge of a fenced field to find its lowest point, you cut straight through the middle, guided by a barrier that keeps you inside.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply IPMs, also called barrier methods, to convex optimisation problems where both theoretical guarantees and practical speed matter. A pitfall is forgetting that, unlike active-set methods such as simplex, IPMs traverse the interior rather than the boundary of the feasible region.
tiers.paperLevel: IPMs solve linear and non-linear convex optimisation problems with polynomial run-time, unlike the simplex method's exponential worst case, and run as fast as simplex in practice, unlike the ellipsoid method's slow practical performance; they traverse the interior of the feasible region rather than its boundary.

explainer.example: A convex problem with many constraints can be solved by an IPM in polynomial time while matching simplex's practical speed, whereas the ellipsoid method would be far slower despite its polynomial guarantee.
